new_statements.translation: 3.6.1. Unlike tone, intensity stress (sound amplitude measured in decibels) has no distinctive function in Ye'pâ-masa. The placement of primary stress depends largely on the emphasis situation. [...] There is a certain tendency to place intensity stress every two moras, with much individual variation according to emphasis [p. 63] || There are two tonic melodies associated with lexemes: the high or register melody, and the rising or contour melody. A third melody, the low melody, is phonologically atonic and characterizes suffixes and dependent words. [p. 15]

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog holds a Tucano record with an empty rule and no statements; Ramirez supplies the type: lexical tone (two tonic melodies vs atonic), with intensity stress explicitly non-distinctive and emphasis-driven.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tucano (Ye'pâ-masa) is a tone language: every lexeme is bimoraic and carries one of two tonic melodies (high/register, written with circumflex on the 2nd mora, or rising/contour, written with acute) or the atonic low melody (suffixes, dependent words); a rising melody's contour tone shifts onto a following non-laryngealized suffix (§3.4.7). Intensity stress is not distinctive: primary stress placement varies with emphasis (u͂yû ['u͂ȷ͂u͂] ~ [u͂'ȷ͂u͂]), with only a tendency to alternate every two moras. Tonal downdrift is the rule (§3.6.2).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only a tendency to place intensity stress every two moras, with much individual variation by emphasis (p. 63, example da'da+bãsí-bı͂ 'he knows how to work'); no fixed secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: About a dozen lexemes with a falling melody [´ `] (§3.4.4, p. 50); some tonally unstable lexemes whose melody changes with morphological context (§3.4.5); laryngealized suffixes block tone shift (§3.4.9); irregular suffixes and dependent words listed in §15.6.
new_statements.identity_note: West & Welch 1967 describe the Acaricuara dialect (Paca River, Papurí basin, Colombia; data 1963-64) and note unhandled vowel changes in the 'downriver dialect'. Ramirez 1997 describes Ye'pâ-masa, the Tukano of the Brazilian Uaupés (Salesian mission area; fieldwork 1994-96). Both are Tucano proper (tuca1252). The archive.org item listed for Longacre & Woods 1976 is a Cuiva (cui, Guahiban) excerpt, not Tucano.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tucano (Acaricuara dialect) has three contrastive pitch levels (high, mid, low) with lexical pitch patterns (minimal pairs díbá 'poison' vs dìbà 'they are', p. 19). Stress is treated as a suprasegmental phoneme alongside pitch and nasalization: monosyllables are stressed; most two- and three-syllable words carry 'multiple stress' with a crescendo rising to the final syllable; words without multiple stress carry a single marked stress; words of four or more syllables peak on the second or third syllable and then fall. No fixed stress position is stated.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'Multiple stress' on di- and trisyllables: crescendo from the first syllable to the ultimate (bupuwɨ 'blowgun', yábá 'deer'); in words of four or more syllables the crescendo reaches the second or third syllable and then decrescendos (ù'búsé?rò 'fingernail', kapé'wérì 'eyebrow').
new_statements.exceptions: Seven minor pitch patterns of limited membership on trisyllables (p. 19); pitch perturbation with certain possessive pronouns; the suffixes /-a/ 'plural' and /-se/ 'nominalizer' have intrinsic stress and high pitch and perturb the word's pitch pattern (p. 19). The authors say the stress and pitch patterns are 'presented in bare outline' pending fuller analysis (p. 11).
new_statements.identity_note: West & Welch 1967 describe the Acaricuara dialect (Paca River, Papurí basin, Colombia; data 1963-64) and note unhandled vowel changes in the 'downriver dialect'. Ramirez 1997 describes Ye'pâ-masa, the Tukano of the Brazilian Uaupés (Salesian mission area; fieldwork 1994-96). Both are Tucano proper (tuca1252). The archive.org item listed for Longacre & Woods 1976 is a Cuiva (cui, Guahiban) excerpt, not Tucano.

readall_conflicts: The two sources actually read agree that lexical pitch/tone, not stress position, is the contrastive prosody of Tucano, and neither gives a fixed stress position. They differ in status and analysis: West & Welch 1967 (Acaricuara dialect, Colombia) treat stress as a phonemic suprasegmental with three contrastive pitch levels and nine two/three-syllable pitch patterns, describing 'multiple stress' as a crescendo to the final syllable and single stress marked lexically on other words; Ramirez 1997 (Ye'pâ-masa, Brazil) states flatly that intensity stress has no distinctive function and varies with emphasis (tendency to every-two-moras alternation), and analyses tone as two tonic melodies (high/register vs rising/contour) on bimoraic lexemes plus an atonic low melody, with tone shift onto suffixes and downdrift. So there is a mild disagreement on whether stress is phonemic at all (1967: yes, marked; 1997: no), and a wholesale difference in the tonal analysis (3 levels/pitch patterns vs 2 melodies + atonic), partly attributable to 30 years of analysis and to dialect. The five SIL/Discourse-grammar works could not be opened (dead SIL Colombia URLs, could not be reached by automated download SIL search, the Internet Archive unreachable, lending-only archive.org copy) and one archive.org item was a Cuiva excerpt.
